missions/africa-faith-missions/name: Faith missions to Africa (Sudan Interior Mission, Africa Inland Mission, Sudan United Mission and others)
missions/africa-faith-missions/origin/na: London and Toronto (main sending centres); Lagos and Mombasa (first landings)
missions/africa-faith-missions/statusNot: SIM (now 'Serving In Mission', after mergers in 1982, 1989 and 1998) and Africa Inland Mission remain large international missions, while the churches they founded — ECWA in Nigeria, the Kale Heywet Church in Ethiopia, the Africa Inland Church in Kenya and Tanzania, the Evangelical Church of Niger and others — are autonomous and themselves send missionaries.
missions/africa-faith-missions/summary: On the model of Hudson Taylor's China Inland Mission, a cluster of interdenominational evangelical 'faith missions' set out between the 1870s and 1910s to evangelise Africa's interior, especially the 'Sudan' belt south of the Sahara and the East African highlands. Premillennial, conservative and largely lay, they suffered terrible early mortality but planted some of the largest evangelical churches in Africa — notably in Nigeria's Middle Belt, southern Ethiopia and Kenya — while also clashing with African culture and becoming entangled with colonial and settler society.
missions/africa-faith-missions/story:
Faith missions came to Africa through the network around Henry Grattan Guinness, whose East London Training Institute (1873) trained hundreds of non-ordained missionaries. Guinness founded the Livingstone Inland Mission to the Congo (1878, handed to American Baptists in 1884), and his circle produced the North Africa Mission (1881) and the Regions Beyond Missionary Union (1899). The South Africa General Mission (1889, later Africa Evangelical Fellowship) was founded by Spencer Walton with Andrew Murray as president. All took the CIM's principles — interdenominational evangelical membership, no guaranteed salaries, field direction and a stress on the unreached interior — and added a sense of urgency fed by premillennial expectation and by the advance of Islam southward across the savannah.

The Sudan Interior Mission began with three young men in Toronto: the Scots-Canadian Walter Gowans, the Canadian Thomas Kent and the English-born Rowland Bingham. Having been refused by established boards, they sailed for Lagos in 1893 intending to reach the vast 'Sudan' between the Atlantic and the Nile, home to tens of millions without any missionary. Gowans died of fever at Girku near Zaria in November 1894 and Kent at Bida a month later; Bingham returned home ill. After further failures, a party in 1901–02 established the first lasting station at Patigi on the Niger. SIM spread through the Middle Belt and north of Nigeria, into Niger (1924), and in 1927 into southern Ethiopia under Thomas Lambie. In Nigeria British indirect rule kept missions out of the Muslim emirates for decades, so SIM churches grew mainly among non-Muslim peoples of the plateau and Middle Belt, coalescing as the Evangelical Church of West Africa (ECWA, 1954), whose Evangelical Missionary Society (1948) became one of Africa's largest indigenous mission agencies. SIM's radio station ELWA in Monrovia (1954) broadcast across West Africa.

Ethiopia produced the most remarkable story. When Italy occupied the country in 1936–37 SIM missionaries were expelled from Wolaitta, leaving a church of about 48 baptised believers; when they returned after the liberation of 1941 they found thousands of believers — commonly cited as around 10,000 — and scores of congregations led by Wolaitta and Kambatta evangelists who had endured imprisonment and flogging. This self-propagating movement grew into the Kale Heywet ('Word of Life') Church, now one of Ethiopia's largest Protestant churches with several million members.

The Africa Inland Mission was founded in 1895 by Peter Cameron Scott, a Scottish-born American who had served with the International Missionary Alliance on the Congo coast. His party landed at Mombasa and opened stations among the Kamba at Nzaui and elsewhere; Scott died at the end of 1896. Under Charles Hurlburt (director 1897–1926) AIM moved to Kijabe on the Rift Valley escarpment (1901–03), founded Rift Valley Academy (1906; Theodore Roosevelt laid a cornerstone in 1909) and Kijabe hospital, and spread into Tanganyika, Uganda, the Belgian Congo (1912), Sudan and later Chad and the Central African Republic. Its Kenyan church became the Africa Inland Church, autonomous from 1943 and fully independent of the mission in 1971; future Kenyan president Daniel arap Moi was educated in AIM schools and remained a member.

Other faith missions followed: the Sudan United Mission (1904), founded by Karl Kumm and Lucy Guinness, worked across the central Sudan belt from northern Nigeria to Chad; C. T. Studd's Heart of Africa Mission (1913, later WEC International) went to north-eastern Congo; Brethren missionaries such as Frederick Stanley Arnot (1881) worked in Katanga and Angola. Together they shared conservative doctrine, opposition to theological liberalism, a reluctance at first to invest in higher education, and a strong emphasis on vernacular Bibles, itinerant evangelism, village churches and, increasingly, hospitals and primary schools.

Their record is mixed. In Kenya AIM joined the Church of Scotland and CMS in the 1929 campaign to make church members renounce female circumcision, which drove many Kikuyu and Kamba into independent churches and schools; AIM's closeness to white settlers and its paternalism slowed African leadership. Missionaries were often hostile to dancing, drinking, polygamy and traditional rites, and slow to hand over property and power. Yet the churches they planted became self-governing, evangelistic and, in many cases, among the largest Protestant bodies on the continent, and after independence they became senders of missionaries themselves.
missions/africa-faith-missions/beliefs/0: Conservative evangelical doctrine: the inerrancy of Scripture, substitutionary atonement, the necessity of personal conversion and the eternal lostness of those without Christ.
missions/africa-faith-missions/beliefs/1: Premillennial urgency: the gospel must be preached as a witness to all nations, especially 'unoccupied fields', before Christ's return.
missions/africa-faith-missions/beliefs/2: The faith principle inherited from the CIM: dependence on God for finance, without guaranteed salaries or public appeals.
missions/africa-faith-missions/beliefs/3: Interdenominational evangelical unity on core doctrines, with church order left largely to field practice (often Baptist or Presbyterian-type congregations).
missions/africa-faith-missions/beliefs/4: A sense of contest with Islam for the 'Sudan' belt and with traditional religion, understood in terms of spiritual warfare.
missions/africa-faith-missions/beliefs/5: A strict separation between church and 'worldly' customs, including alcohol, polygamy, dancing and initiation rites.
missions/africa-faith-missions/strategie: Pioneering chains of stations into the interior — SIM across the Sudan belt, AIM in a line from Mombasa toward Lake Chad in Scott's vision.
Training African evangelists and pastors in Bible schools rather than (at first) in universities.
Vernacular translation, literacy and Bible distribution in Hausa, Nupe, Yoruba, Wolaitta, Kamba, Kalenjin and many other languages.
Medical work: SIM hospitals such as Egbe and Jos Evangel Hospital in Nigeria and AIM's Kijabe hospital in Kenya.
Radio and literature: SIM's ELWA (1954) and the African Challenge magazine.
Schools for missionaries' children (Rift Valley Academy, Kent Academy) to sustain long-term family service.
Encouraging African churches to send their own missionaries, as in ECWA's Evangelical Missionary Society (1948).
missions/africa-faith-missions/groupsRea: Peoples of Nigeria's Middle Belt and plateau — Tiv, Berom, Gbagyi, Yoruba of Kwara, Nupe and many others — who formed the core of ECWA.
The Wolaitta, Kambatta, Hadiya, Gedeo and Sidama of southern Ethiopia.
Kamba, Kalenjin, Maasai and Kikuyu of Kenya; Sukuma and other peoples of Tanzania.
Peoples of north-eastern Congo, southern Sudan, Chad and the Central African Republic.
Hausa and Fulani Muslims and Tuareg in Niger, among whom conversions were few.
missions/africa-faith-missions/challenge: Extreme early mortality — two of SIM's three founders died within a year, and Peter Cameron Scott within fourteen months.
Colonial restrictions, notably in northern Nigeria, where British indirect rule barred missions from Muslim emirates for decades.
The Italian occupation of Ethiopia (1936–41) and later the Marxist Derg regime (1974–91), which imprisoned church leaders and seized property.
Resistance from Muslim rulers and populations across the Sahel.
Recurrent tension between missionary control and African leaders seeking autonomy and education.
missions/africa-faith-missions/harms/0: The 1929 female circumcision campaign in Kenya, joined by AIM, was experienced as an assault on community identity and fuelled division and resentment.
missions/africa-faith-missions/harms/1: AIM's close ties with settler society and colonial officials in Kenya associated the mission with racial hierarchy and land alienation.
missions/africa-faith-missions/harms/2: Hostility to African music, dance and rites, and to polygamists seeking baptism, caused social disruption and drove many to independent churches.
missions/africa-faith-missions/harms/3: Reluctance to provide secondary and higher education left African Christians disadvantaged relative to those in denominational missions.
missions/africa-faith-missions/harms/4: Mission-reinforced religious boundaries in Nigeria's Middle Belt became part of the background to later Christian–Muslim tensions.
missions/africa-faith-missions/harms/5: Slow transfer of property and leadership, often only completed in the 1970s.
missions/africa-faith-missions/developme: Some of Africa's largest evangelical churches: ECWA in Nigeria, the Kale Heywet Church in Ethiopia and the Africa Inland Church in Kenya and Tanzania.
The Wolaitta revival of 1937–41, a celebrated case of a church growing without missionaries under persecution.
Major hospitals, schools and Bible colleges across West and East Africa.
Vernacular literature and Bible translations in dozens of African languages.
African mission agencies, such as ECWA's Evangelical Missionary Society, among the largest indigenous sending bodies in Africa.
Christian radio broadcasting from ELWA in Liberia across the continent.
missions/africa-faith-missions/outcome: From disastrous beginnings the African faith missions grew into large international agencies and, more importantly, planted self-governing evangelical churches numbering many millions, which now send missionaries of their own. Their history includes both remarkable indigenous growth and serious cultural and colonial entanglements.

missions/africa-faith-missions/countries: SIM's founders landed at Lagos; the first lasting station opened at Patigi (1902), leading to ECWA and hospitals at Egbe and Jos.
AIM's first stations among the Kamba; Kijabe headquarters, Rift Valley Academy and the Africa Inland Church.
The Livingstone Inland Mission (1878), AIM (1912) and the Heart of Africa Mission (1913) worked in western and north-eastern Congo.
SIM opened work among Hausa, Fulani and others; the Evangelical Church of Niger grew slowly in a Muslim society.

missions/africa-faith-missions/journeys/: Walter Gowans, Thomas Kent and Rowland Bingham
The three sailed via England to Lagos in December 1893. Gowans and Kent set off for the interior while Bingham stayed at the coast; Gowans died at Girku and Kent at Bida in late 1894.
Peter Cameron Scott and the AIM party (1895–96)
Peter Cameron Scott and the first AIM party
Scott's party landed at Mombasa in October 1895 and walked inland, founding stations at Nzaui, Sakai, Kilungu and Kangundo before Scott's death in December 1896.
Thomas Lambie and the first SIM Ethiopia party
With permission from Ras Tafari (later Haile Selassie), the party travelled south from Addis Ababa to open stations among the Kambatta, Hadiya and Wolaitta.
missions/africa-faith-missions/relations: ECWA's Evangelical Missionary Society (1948) and Ethiopian Kale Heywet evangelists were early examples of African-led cross-cultural mission.
Worked with Bible societies and later Wycliffe/SIL on vernacular translation across West and East Africa.
SIM and AIM were prominent in post-war evangelical mission networks such as the IFMA and the Lausanne movement.
missions/africa-faith-missions/agreement: Adopted the CIM's faith principle, field direction, interdenominational evangelical basis and focus on unreached interiors.
Joined Scottish and CMS missions in Kenya in the 1929 stand against female circumcision.
Shared the evangelical commitment to evangelising unreached peoples and to biblical authority.
missions/africa-faith-missions/disagreem: Rejected the theological liberalism they perceived in the International Missionary Council and later the WCC; most faith missions joined the separate Interdenominational Foreign Mission Association (1917) instead.
Opposed African independent and prophet churches over polygamy, healing practices and traditional rites; many independent churches in Kenya arose in reaction to mission policy in 1929–31.
Faith missions criticised denominational boards for institutionalism and comity agreements that, they argued, left the interior unevangelised.
missions/africa-faith-missions/deviation: Founded as lean pioneering movements, they became large institutional missions with hospitals, schools and radio stations.
The ideal of rapid evangelism and moving on gave way to decades of missionary control before transfer to African churches.
Initial resistance to higher education was reversed after the 1950s as African churches demanded it.
